claims.text: The initial lightweight high-entropy alloy has a density below 7 g/cm^3.
The intervention is an addition of 0.1–0.5 wt% boron.
The hypothesis is expected to hold when the alloy is processed by mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering.
Boron is introduced in the form of B4C nanoparticles.
The intervention forms a boron-rich grain-boundary phase.
The boron-rich grain-boundary phase enhances grain-boundary cohesion.
The boron-rich grain-boundary phase reduces oxidation and corrosion pathways.
The boron-rich grain-boundary phase reduces oxygen diffusion along grain boundaries.
The boron-rich grain-boundary phase reduces diffusion of corrosive species along grain boundaries.
Boron addition causes grain refinement.
Boron addition produces precipitation hardening.
Grain refinement and precipitation hardening enhance alloy strength and toughness.
The boron-modified alloy has higher room-temperature yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
The boron-modified alloy has higher room-temperature ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified alloy.
The boron-modified alloy has greater room-temperature elongation than the unmodified alloy.
The boron-modified alloy has better saltwater corrosion resistance than the unmodified alloy.
The boron-modified alloy has better high-temperature oxidation resistance in air than the unmodified alloy.
After boron modification, the alloy density remains below 7 g/cm^3.
The boron addition does not form brittle phases.
The boron addition does not cause excessive grain growth.

contradictions.description: The baseline is said to have the same composition as the modified alloy, but adding 0.1–0.5 wt% boron necessarily changes composition. The intended control is presumably the same parent composition and processing history except for the boron/B4C addition.
